'''Aleš Strojnik''' (also known as '''Alex Strojnik''', May 21, 1921 – November 6, 1995)<ref>{{cite web|title=Ales Strojnik 1921-1995|url=http://www.ancientfaces.com/person/ales-strojnik/17126695|website=ancientfaces.com|access-date=16 January 2015}}</ref> was a [[Slovenian American]] aerodynamicist and aircraft designer specializing in low-speed drag reduction. He was also a pioneer and professor in physics and high-energy electron microscopy,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hawkes|first1=Peter|title=Cold field emission and the scanning transmission electron microscope|journal=Advances in Imaging and Electron Physics|date=2009|volume=159|page=405}}<br>- {{cite journal|title=Slovenian American inventors and innovators|journal=Slovenian American Times|date=October 16, 2013|volume=V|issue=12|page=13|url=http://www.kamnik-tourism.si/assets/PDF-FILES/SA-TIMES-proof.pdf|access-date=January 19, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150119215441/http://www.kamnik-tourism.si/assets/PDF-FILES/SA-TIMES-proof.pdf|archive-date=January 19, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> and retired from teaching and research at [[Arizona State University]] in [[Tempe, Arizona]].<ref>{{cite web|title=ASU general catalog, 1971-1973|url=http://repository.asu.edu/attachments/105244/content/ASU_General_Catalog_1971-1973_pp_151-300.pdf|website=repository.asu.edu|publisher=Arizona State University|access-date=January 16, 2015}}</ref> His daughter, [[Marija Strojnik Scholl]], took interest in [[optics]] at an early age when she was accompanying her father to work, and went on to become a prominent [[astrophysicist]].<ref name="Delo">{{cite news|last=Bandur|first=Simona|date=May 23, 2018|title=Znanstvenica, ki sledi svoji otroški želji po odkrivanju prostora|language=sl|trans-title=A scientist who follows her childhood wish to explore space|work=[[Delo (Slovenia)|Delo]]|url=https://www.delo.si/magazin/zanimivosti/znanstvenica-ki-sledi-svoji-otroski-zelji-po-odkrivanju-prostora-53268.html|access-date=April 24, 2019}}</ref>

Strojnik was born and educated in [[Ljubljana]], [[Slovenia]], [[Yugoslavia]]. He was imprisoned at the [[Gonars concentration camp]] during [[World War II]] along with thousands of other ethnic Slovenes by the [[Fascist]] Italian authorities of the [[Province of Ljubljana]]. After the war, Strojnik returned to academia and research. He is called by some "the first Slovenian biomedical engineer", and he was influential in cultivating a sense of quality among his students.<ref>{{cite web|title=Honorary members|url=http://www.dmbts.si/society.php?lang=eng&item=3|website=dmbts.si|publisher=Slovenian Society for Medical and Biomedical Engineering|access-date=January 21, 2015}}</ref>

Strojnik had some training in, and passion for, [[aeronautical engineering]]. His first aircraft design, which he built in Slovenia (then part of [[Yugoslavia]]) in 1945, was called the S-1. It was a [[flying-wing]] [[glider (sailplane)|glider]]. After suffering a fractured skull and broken nose in crashing the S-1, he abandoned the design.<ref>{{cite journal|title=A touch of magic|journal=Kitplanes|date=April 1990|pages=18–20}}</ref>

Strojnik's pursuit of quality in science landed him on the wrong side of Slovenian academia, controlled after the war by the [[Yugoslav Partisans]] of [[Josip Broz Tito]]'s postwar [[Communist]] government. Strojnik's article "Who Is a Scientist" appeared in the communist publication ''Nova Obzorja'' (New Horizon).<ref>{{cite book|last1=Bevc|first1=Ladislav|title=Liberal Forces in Twentieth Century Yugoslavia: Memoirs of Ladislav Bevc|date=2007|publisher=Peter Lang Publishing Inc|location=New York, NY|isbn=978-1-4331-0008-6|page=276}}</ref>

<blockquote>That article made [Strojnik] universally resented in the Slovenian academic circles because it exposed the rotten core of the Slovenian academia. It was advisable for Strojnik to look for employment abroad...The result was a visiting appointment for Strojnik at Cornell University in electron microscopy. Later Strojnik became full professor at the Arizona State University in Tempe.</blockquote>

In addition to his academic career, after immigrating to the United States, Strojnik continued the pursuit of his passion for aviation and aircraft design. The [[Strojnik S-2]] self-launching sailplane, the S-4 and S-5 sport planes, and Strojnik's ''Laminar Aircraft'' three-volume book series had great impact on light aircraft design. The S-4 "Laminar Magic" set a U.S. national aviation speed record in [[Fédération Aéronautique Internationale]] (FAI) Category C-1a/0 (European [[microlight]], under {{convert|300|kg|lb}} gross weight) in 1987.<ref>{{cite news|title=Sport Aviation|issue=November 1989|publisher=Experimental Aircraft Association|date=November 10, 1989}}</ref> Strojnik also wrote a much earlier book entitled ''Človek je dobil krila'' ("Man Got His Wings") in Slovene, which was published in 1947.<ref>{{cite book|title=Človek je dobil krila|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Y9HyOQAACAAJ |website=Google |access-date=16 January 2015|last1 = Strojnik|first1 = Aleš|year = 1947}}<br>- {{cite web|title=Does someone know the books of Alex Strojnik|url=http://www.homebuiltairplanes.com/forums/aircraft-design-aerodynamics-new-technology/13087-does-someone-know-books-alex-strojnik-low-power-laminar-aircraft-structures-2.html|website=Homebuilt Airplanes|access-date=January 16, 2015|archive-url=https://archive.today/20150119044117/http://www.homebuiltairplanes.com/forums/aircraft-design-aerodynamics-new-technology/13087-does-someone-know-books-alex-strojnik-low-power-laminar-aircraft-structures-2.html|archive-date=January 19, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Strojnik had four sons and a daughter.
